title: Synchronous vs Asynchronous Communication
description: Understand the trade-offs between synchronous request-response and asynchronous message-based communication.

data.text: Communication style fundamentally affects system resilience and scalability. Synchronous communication is simple but couples services tightly. Asynchronous communication is more resilient but adds complexity. Netflix and Uber use both, depending on the use case.

In synchronous communication, the caller waits for the callee to respond before continuing. This is the simplest model and works well for request-response scenarios like fetching user data. However, if the callee is slow or down, the caller is blocked.

data.title: Synchronous Characteristics
items: Temporal coupling: both services must be available
Examples: REST APIs, gRPC calls, database queries

data.text: In asynchronous communication, the caller sends a message and continues without waiting. The callee processes the message later. This decouples services in time and space, making the system more resilient. Examples include message queues (RabbitMQ, Kafka) and event streams.

data.title: Asynchronous Characteristics
items: Caller does not wait for response
Requires message brokers or event streams
Examples: Kafka, RabbitMQ, AWS SQS, Azure Service Bus

data.title: Cascading Failures
data.text: Synchronous communication can cause cascading failures. If Service A calls Service B synchronously and Service B is slow, Service A's threads get blocked, eventually timing out and failing. This can bring down the entire system.

data.title: Example: Synchronous Order Processing
data.content: A naive order flow might call inventory, payment, and shipping synchronously. If any service is down, the order fails.
data.code:
# Synchronous order processing (bad)
# Order Service --> Inventory Service (blocking)
# Order Service --> Payment Service (blocking)
# Order Service --> Shipping Service (blocking)
#
# Problem: If Payment is down, no orders can be placed
#
# Asynchronous alternative:
# Order Service --> Order Created Event
# Inventory Service listens and reserves stock
# Payment Service listens and processes payment
# Shipping Service listens and ships order

data.definition:
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant A as Service A
    participant B as Service B
    C->>A: Request
    A->>B: Synchronous Call
    B-->>A: Response
    A-->>C: Response

items.question: Should I use synchronous or asynchronous?
items.answer: Use synchronous for simple request-response where you need immediate feedback. Use asynchronous for fire-and-forget, background processing, or when services must remain available.

items.question: Can I mix both?
items.answer: Yes. Most systems use both. Use synchronous for reads and immediate operations, and asynchronous for writes and background processing.

items.question: What about eventual consistency?
items.answer: Asynchronous communication naturally leads to eventual consistency. Data may be temporarily inconsistent but will converge over time.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Synchronous is simple but couples services in time
Asynchronous is resilient but more complex
Use asynchronous for background processing and resilience
data.takeaway: Prefer asynchronous communication when possible; it makes your system more resilient to failures.
